blocks.p: Now when the Shepherds saw so great a train following Mr. Great-heart, for they knew him well, they said to him, “Good sir, you have a fine company here. Pray, where did you find them all?”
Then Mr. Great-heart replied:

v: First, here is Christiana and her train,
her sons and their wives, like sailors on
the main,
who’ve kept the pole star, steering by it
clear
from sin to grace, or they would not be
here.
Next, here’s old Honest, come on
pilgrimage;
and Ready-to-stumble, who, I will engage,
is true of heart; and so is Feeble-mind,
who was not willing to be left behind.
Despondency, good man, is coming after,
and with him Much-afraid, his trembling daughter.
May we find welcome here, or must we go
still further on? Tell us, so we may know.

blocks.p: “This is a comfortable company,” said the Shepherds. “You are welcome to us, for we have comfort for the feeble as well as for the strong. Our Prince has an eye to what is done to the least of these, so infirmity must be no bar to our hospitality.” [Matt. 25:40] So they led them to the palace door, and then they said, “Come in, Mr. Feeble-mind. Come in, Mr. Ready-to-stumble. Come in, Mr. Despondency, and Mrs. Much-afraid, his daughter. These, Mr. Great-heart,” the Shepherds said to the guide, “we call in by name, because they are the most likely to draw back; but as for you and the rest who are strong, we leave you to your usual liberty.”

“Today I see that grace shines in your faces,” said Mr. Great-heart, “and that you are my Lord’s Shepherds indeed; for you have not shoved these ailing ones aside with flank or shoulder, but have rather strewn their way into the palace with flowers, as you should.” [Ezek. 34:21]

So the feeble and the weak went in, and Mr. Great-heart and the rest followed. When they were seated, the Shepherds said to the weaker ones, “What is it you would like? For everything here,” they said, “must be managed for the support of the weak as well as the warning of the unruly.”
So they made them a feast of things easy to digest, pleasant to the taste, and nourishing; and when they had eaten, they went to their rest, each to his proper place.

When morning came, because the mountains were high and the day was clear, and because it was the Shepherds’ custom to show pilgrims some rarities before they left, they took them out into the fields after they had readied and refreshed themselves, and showed them first what they had shown Christian before. Then they took them to some new places. The first was Mount Marvel, where they looked and saw a man in the distance tumbling the hills about with words. They asked the Shepherds what this meant, and they told them that the man was a son of Great-grace, of whom you read in the First Part of the Records of the Pilgrim’s Progress, and that he is set there to teach pilgrims how to believe down, or tumble out of their way by faith, whatever difficulties they meet. [Mark 11:23-24]
“I know him,” said Mr. Great-heart. “He is a man above many.”

Then they took them to another place, called Mount Innocent, where they saw a man dressed all in white, and two men, Prejudice and Ill-will, continually throwing dirt at him. But whatever dirt they threw at him would fall off again in a little while, and his clothes would look as clean as if no dirt had ever been thrown.
“What does this mean?” said the pilgrims.

“This man is named Godly-man,” the Shepherds answered, “and this garment is to show the innocence of his life. Those who throw dirt at him are the ones who hate his good conduct; but as you see that the dirt will not stick to his clothes, so it will be with the man who lives truly innocent in the world. Whoever would make such men dirty labors in vain; for in a little time God will cause their innocence to break out like the light and their righteousness like the noonday.”

Then they took them to Mount Charity, where they showed them a man with a bundle of cloth lying in front of him, out of which he cut coats and garments for the poor who stood around him; yet his bundle, or roll of cloth, never grew any smaller.
“What is this?” they said.

“This is to show you,” said the Shepherds, “that he who has a heart to give his labor to the poor will never lack the means to do it. He who waters will be watered himself; and the cake the widow gave the Prophet did not leave her any the less in her barrel.”

They also took them to a place where they saw two men, Fool and Want-wit, washing an Ethiopian with the intention of making him white; but the more they washed him, the blacker he grew. They asked the Shepherds what that meant.

“So it is with the vile person,” they said. “Every means used to get such a man a good name will, in the end, only make him more loathsome. So it was with the Pharisees, and so it will be with all hypocrites.”

Then Mercy, Matthew’s wife, said to Christiana her mother, “Mother, if it might be allowed, I would like to see the hole in the hill, the one they call the byway to hell.” So her mother put the request to the Shepherds, and they went to the door. It was in the side of a hill. They opened it and told Mercy to listen a while. So she listened, and heard one voice saying, “Cursed be my father, for holding my feet back from the way of peace and life”; and another saying, “Oh, that I had been torn to pieces before I lost my soul to save my life!”; and another, “If I had my life to live again, how I would deny myself rather than come to this place!” Then it was as if the very earth groaned and quaked under the young woman’s feet with fear. She turned white and came away trembling, saying, “Blessed be he and she that are delivered from this place.”

When the Shepherds had shown them all these things, they took them back to the palace and entertained them with what the house could offer. But Mercy, being young and expecting a child, longed for something she had seen there, and was ashamed to ask for it. Her mother-in-law asked her what was the matter, for she looked like someone unwell.
“There is a mirror hanging in the dining room,” said Mercy, “and I cannot get my mind off it. If I don’t have it, I think I shall miscarry.”
“I will mention your wish to the Shepherds,” said her mother, “and they will not deny it to you.”
“But I am ashamed that these men should know I longed for it.”
“No, my daughter. It is no shame but a virtue to long for a thing like that.”
“Then, Mother, if you please, ask the Shepherds whether they are willing to sell it.”

Now this mirror was one in a thousand. Held one way, it would show a man his own features exactly [James 1:23]; but turn it the other way, and it would show the very face and likeness of the Prince of Pilgrims himself. [1 Cor. 13:12] Yes, I have talked with people who can tell, and they have said that by looking in that glass they have seen the very crown of thorns on his head; they have also seen in it the holes in his hands, in his feet, and in his side. [2 Cor. 3:18] Such is the excellence of that glass that it will show him to anyone in whatever way they have a mind to see him: living or dead, on earth or in heaven, in his humiliation or in his exaltation, coming to suffer or coming to reign.

So Christiana went to the Shepherds privately (now the names of the Shepherds are Knowledge, Experience, Watchful, and Sincere) and said to them, “One of my daughters, who is expecting a child, longs, I think, for something she has seen in this house; and she believes she will miscarry if you deny it to her.”

“Call her, call her,” said Experience. “She shall certainly have whatever we can help her to.” So they called her and said, “Mercy, what is it you would like?” She blushed, and said, “The great mirror that hangs in the dining room.” So Sincere ran and fetched it, and with glad consent it was given to her. Then she bowed her head and gave thanks, and said, “By this I know that I have found favor in your eyes.”
They also gave the other young women the things they desired, and gave their husbands great commendation for having joined Mr. Great-heart in slaying Giant Despair and demolishing Doubting Castle.
The Shepherds put a bracelet around Christiana’s neck, and the same around the necks of her four daughters; they also put earrings in their ears and jewels on their foreheads.

When they were ready to leave, the Shepherds let them go in peace, but did not give them the particular warnings that had been given to Christian and his companion. The reason was that these pilgrims had Great-heart for their guide, a man well acquainted with the way, who could give them their warnings at the right moment, that is, just when the danger was approaching. Christian and his companion had lost the warnings the Shepherds gave them by the time they needed to put them into practice; so here this company had the advantage over the other.
From here they went on singing, and this is what they sang:

v: See how the stages have been fitly set
for the relief of those who pilgrims have become,
how they receive us, with no hindrance met,
who make the other life our aim and home!
What novelties they have, to us they give,
that we, though pilgrims, may with gladness live;
and such things, too, they put upon us here
as show we’re pilgrims wherever we appear.
